tagline: From Baker, a paved desert road leads toward Great Basin National Park
intro: Lehman Caves Road runs west from Baker through desert country toward Great Basin National Park, roughly following Lehman Creek uphill. The National Park Service directs drivers five miles west on Highway 488 to reach the park. Nevada’s Department of Transportation designated SR 488 a Nevada Scenic Byway on March 27, 2000. Sagebrush, saltbush, pinyon and Utah juniper dominate the area near the visitor center.

The caves were protected as a national monument in 1922; that monument became part of Great Basin National Park in 1986. An earlier unimproved route appears on Nevada highway maps by 1937, meeting Baker Road north of town. By 1942, State Route 74 followed the present alignment through Baker; gravel surfacing followed by 1948 and paving by 1949. The statewide renumbering replaced SR 74 with SR 488 in 1976. The 1978–79 state highway map was the first to show the new number.

Begin in Baker at the junction of Routes 487 and 488, then follow Lehman Caves Road west. The numbered state route reaches its western endpoint at a cattle guard, 0.707 miles east of the Lehman Caves Visitor Center. Continue toward the center, where Lehman’s orchard and a partly reconstructed irrigation ditch record an earlier use of this ground.

moments.title: Baker
moments.text: Baker sits at the junction of Routes 487 and 488, five miles east of Great Basin National Park’s main entrance. The park’s Great Basin Visitor Center is here on Route 487. Inside is a rifle recovered from the park in 2014, leaning against a juniper tree. Archaeologist Eva Jensen found the gun during a search for artifacts before a project to reduce wildfire fuels. Manufactured in 1882, the Winchester has no known story explaining its abandonment. X-rays during conservation revealed a cartridge hidden in the buttstock, made between 1887 and 1911. The rifle and cartridge are displayed together.

moments.title: Lehman Caves
moments.text: Absalom Lehman began guiding visitors into the caves in 1885, but Indigenous people knew them before Europeans arrived. Visitors left inscriptions before the caves became a national monument in 1922. The monument became part of Great Basin National Park in 1986. Lehman also planted an orchard and brought irrigation water two miles from Lehman Creek. The orchard had more than 100 trees at its peak; its 1930s plantings included pears, plums, crabapples and apples, alongside peaches and apricots. Near the visitor center, seven apricot trees and one peach tree remain, along with a reconstructed portion of the ditch.

moments.title: Wheeler Peak
moments.text: Wheeler Peak reaches an elevation of 13,063 feet within Great Basin National Park. At treeline near the peak grew Prometheus, a Great Basin bristlecone pine at least 5,000 years old. A graduate student and U.S. Forest Service personnel cut it down for research in 1964. The park protects groves of ancient bristlecone pines, while its higher elevations also support meadows, white fir and quaking aspen. At treeline, low alpine plants grow among rocky outcrops. The summit trail begins at 10,160 feet, already high above the desert. The Wheeler summit trail is strenuous, and its altitude can challenge unprepared hikers.

practical: Baker: The National Park Service warns that navigation apps can send drivers to remote park locations. Route to Lehman Caves Visitor Center, Great Basin Visitor Center or Baker. (checked 2026-10-11)
